sections.title: Le livre et la bouche
sections.body: Le passé simple, c’est le passé composé des livres : tu le lis, tu ne le dis pas. Tu as repris le décor et l'action de les leçons 3 et 4 du B1, les incises de la leçon 21 du B1, la lecture du sens de la leçon 37 du B1 et le plus-que-parfait de la leçon 1 du B2, et tu les retrouves maintenant dans les livres : tu repères, tu traduis, tu comprends. La suite du B2 reste dans les livres : le subjonctif littéraire, que tu apprendras lui aussi à reconnaître sans jamais le produire. EN: Next in B2 stays in books: the literary subjunctive, which you will also learn to recognise without producing it.
points: Le passé simple vit dans le récit écrit, jamais à l’oral.
Quatre finales, douze irréguliers, et le participe comme clé.
Le passé simple devant, l’imparfait derrière.
Pour raconter : passé composé, et rien d’autre ne bouge.
sections.say: Le passé simple, c’est le passé composé des livres : tu le lis, tu ne le dis pas.

recorded.desc: The tale « Le meunier et la graine » (act 1), one warm storyteller voice, one take, the pace of a bedtime story. The passé simple forms are read with no emphasis: the learner is meant to notice them, not be told. Rose's line and the traveller's words in quotation marks are spoken lightly in character.

Tom and Julie at the coffee machine (act 2), two voices: Tom with a light English accent reading his passé simple lines a little proudly; Julie, a Montréal colleague, amused and friendly. One take, conversational pace.
The four genre cards (act 2). One voice. Each card line is read in the register of its genre: storyteller, history teacher, biographer, radio documentary.
The history textbook page (act 2), one clear teacher voice, one take, the pace of a lesson read aloud. Dates are read in full (mille six cent huit).

Awa reads her grandfather's travel notebook to her grandmother (act 3), two female voices, warm Dakar French. Awa reads the notebook lines slowly, as someone deciphering handwriting; the grandmother answers simply.
The four -er cards (act 3). One voice. Card four reads parla, parlait, parlera with IDENTICAL rhythm and pitch, so only the endings differ.

REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, lines in authored order, at natural B2 speed. Eight lines. Lines one to three (parla, parlait, parlera) carry the contrast the questions ask about: read them exactly like the others.
The audio step plays each card's CORRECT modern retelling (passé composé). Six lines, one voice. The wrong readings in promptSound are NEVER spoken.
The Timbuktu travel paragraph (act 3), one voice, read as a page of a book at an unhurried literary pace. Every passé simple is read exactly as written, never modernised and never stressed.
The four -it cards (act 4). One voice. Card four (tous les soirs, il finit) is read as an ordinary present, with no hint that it could be anything else.
The prince and the key (act 4), one voice, read as a page of a book at an unhurried literary pace. Every passé simple is read exactly as written, never modernised and never stressed.
Noé and his tutor Mme Aubert in Geneva (act 5), two voices: a teenager hesitating over the book's lines, a calm Swiss tutor. One take.
The four -ut cards (act 5). One voice. Read each form so it can be heard beside its participle: lut like lu, reçut like reçu.

REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, lines in authored order, at natural B2 speed. Eight lines; the last one is in the passé composé and must sound like ordinary speech, not like a book.
Claire's letter (act 5), one voice, read as a page of a book at an unhurried literary pace. Every passé simple is read exactly as written, never modernised and never stressed.
The four -int cards (act 6). One voice. Card one: vint must sound exactly like vingt.
The audio step plays each card's CORRECT modern retelling. Six lines, one voice. The wrong versions (vingt inconnus, ont revenu) are NEVER spoken.
The wolves in winter (act 6), one voice, read as a page of a book at an unhurried literary pace. Every passé simple is read exactly as written, never modernised and never stressed.
Hortense Vallier's biography (act 7), one voice in the tone of a museum audio guide, one take. Dates in full. The final quotation from her notebooks is read a little slower.

REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, lines in authored order, at natural B2 speed. Nine lines of irregular passé simple; the questions ask about content (what, where, when), so no form may be slowed down.
The barn fire (act 7), one voice, read as a page of a book at an unhurried literary pace. Every passé simple is read exactly as written, never modernised and never stressed.
Chloé and her neighbour M. Bertrand in Lausanne (act 8), two voices: a young woman reading the novel's lines, a retired teacher explaining kindly. One take.
The four person cards (act 8). One voice. Card four (tu parlas, vous parlâtes) is read as a curiosity, lightly.
The train to Geneva (act 8), one voice, read as a page of a book at an unhurried literary pace. Every passé simple is read exactly as written, never modernised and never stressed.
The novel page « La lettre » (act 9), one voice, one take, a slow and restrained literary reading. The single line of the letter is read quietly. No sob on « Elle ne pleura pas ».
The four foreground and background cards (act 9). One voice. Card four reads il savait and il sut with the same rhythm.

REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, lines in authored order, at natural B2 speed. Nine lines; the last two are B1 background lines in the imparfait and must not sound different from the others.
The audio step plays each card's CORRECT modern retelling. Six lines, one voice. The wrong versions (il a plu depuis, la porte claquait) are NEVER spoken.
The concert (act 9), one voice, read as a page of a book at an unhurried literary pace. Every passé simple is read exactly as written, never modernised and never stressed.

The Berlin press retrospective (act 10), one voice in the style of a radio documentary, one take. The spokesman's words and the Berlin woman's closing quotation are read by the same narrator, lightly set apart.
The Tennis Court Oath (act 10), one voice, read as a page of a book at an unhurried literary pace. Every passé simple is read exactly as written, never modernised and never stressed.

The memoir extract « L'été de mes douze ans » (act 11), one male voice, one take, dry and gently ironic, as a writer reading his own book. The last two sentences, in the present-day passé composé, change tone slightly: the adult speaking now.
The four reading-question cards (act 11). One voice, the tone of an exam coach.

REQUIRED FOR THE EAR MISSION: ONE TAKE, ONE VOICE, lines in authored order, at natural B2 speed. Eight lines read like a radio reading of a novel; the questions are about meaning, so no line is dramatised.

The surprise test, with its irony audible but never underlined (act 11), one voice, read as a page of a book at an unhurried literary pace. Every passé simple is read exactly as written, never modernised and never stressed.

Léa's message to Hugo (act 12), one young female voice, one take, read as a voice message to a friend: natural, quick, warm. It must sound like speech, because the point is that it contains no passé simple.
